## Observations

1. An \(M \times M\) subgrid fits inside \(S\) exactly when its top-left row and column are both between \(1\) and \(N-M+1\), inclusive.
2. A candidate matches \(T\) only if every pair of corresponding cells has the same character; one mismatch is enough to reject it.
3. Exactly one candidate matches, so the search can stop at the first full match.
4. There are \((N-M+1)^2\) candidates, each requiring at most \(M^2\) cell comparisons, so direct search is fast enough for \(N \le 50\).

## Solution sketch

1. > An \(M \times M\) subgrid fits inside \(S\) exactly when its top-left row and column are both between \(1\) and \(N-M+1\), inclusive.

   Read the dimensions and store both grids as rows of characters. Visit every valid top-left position \((a,b)\) in row-major order, using the inclusive bounds above. When \(M=N\), this visits only \((1,1)\).

2. > A candidate matches \(T\) only if every pair of corresponding cells has the same character; one mismatch is enough to reject it.

   For each candidate, compare \(T_{i,j}\) with \(S_{a+i-1,b+j-1}\) for all rows and columns of \(T\). Move to the next candidate as soon as a character differs. When \(M=1\), each candidate requires just one comparison.

3. > Exactly one candidate matches, so the search can stop at the first full match.

   If all comparisons for a candidate succeed, print its 1-based row and column, separated by a space, and stop. The uniqueness guarantee means no fallback output is needed.

4. > There are \((N-M+1)^2\) candidates, each requiring at most \(M^2\) cell comparisons, so direct search is fast enough for \(N \le 50\).

   The worst-case search time is \(O((N-M+1)^2M^2)\), in addition to \(O(N^2+M^2)\) time to read the grids. Storing the grids takes \(O(N^2+M^2)\) space, and the search uses \(O(1)\) extra space.
